c.tagline: Gateway to Costa Rica's volcanoes, cloud forests, and coasts.

taxi.color: red (official taxis, orange for airport taxis)
taxi.fareNote: Official red taxis ("marchamo") use a meter called la María by law; airport taxis are orange and also metered; always confirm the meter is running or agree on rideshare pricing via app to avoid overcharging.

emergency.note: 911 is the unified national emergency number for police, fire, and medical (Cruz Roja); Hospital CIMA and Hospital Clínica Bíblica are top private hospitals used by visitors.

avoid.reason: Caution around the Coca-Cola bus terminal and downtown at night; some barrios (León XIII, Pavas) higher-crime

hood_desc: Historic downtown core (Barrio Amón/Barrio Otoya) with museums, theaters, colonial-era mansions and budget-to-midrange lodging; best for culture-focused travelers who don't mind gritty streets and want to walk to sights, though caution is needed after dark.
San José's foodie and nightlife district, packed with craft breweries, cafes and top restaurants in a leafy, walkable grid; suits travelers who want a trendy, youthful base close to downtown.
An upscale, palm-lined suburb west of the center with malls, international restaurants and gated condos; ideal for business travelers, families and those wanting safety and comfort over local color.

A quieter, affluent suburban area near Sabana Park and Paseo Colón with embassies, corporate offices and boutique hotels; good for travelers wanting green space, golf-course-turned-park jogging and easy airport access via highway.

A residential, university district (near UCR) with a strong backpacker and student scene, cheap eats and a more local, low-key vibe; suits budget travelers and those wanting an authentic, non-touristy base.

water.note: Tap water in San José and most of the Central Valley is treated and safe to drink.

transit.pay: Buses are paid in cash (colones) directly to the driver on boarding, exact change appreciated; the INCOFER commuter train is also paid in cash on board or at select stations. There is no unified rechargeable transit card system citywide, though some routes are piloting prepaid cards.
transit.hours: Buses run roughly 5am-10pm on most routes with limited frequency late at night; the commuter train operates mainly during weekday peak hours with limited weekend service; no true 24-hour public transit exists, so taxis/rideshare are used at night.
transit.note: Public transit is functional for locals but can be confusing for visitors; most tourists rely on rideshare apps (Uber), official red taxis, or private shuttles for inter-city and airport trips.

tip.r: 10% service charge is often already included on restaurant bills by law; additional tipping is appreciated but not obligatory.

landmarks: Teatro Nacional de Costa Rica
This opulent neoclassical opera house, funded by coffee barons, is San José's crown jewel and a symbol of the nation's cultural aspirations.
Metropolitan Cathedral of San José
The city's principal Catholic church combines neoclassical grandeur with a richly decorated interior, anchoring the historic downtown core.
Museo del Oro Precolombino
Buried beneath the Plaza de la Cultura, this underground museum dazzles with thousands of gleaming pre-Columbian gold artifacts crafted by ancient cultures.
Museo del Jade
Home to the world's largest collection of American jade, this striking modern museum showcases intricately carved pre-Columbian treasures.
Plaza de la Cultura
This bustling central plaza links the National Theatre and Gold Museum, making it a favorite gathering spot and starting point for exploring downtown.
Mercado Central
This labyrinthine covered market has served locals since 1880, offering spices, sodas, souvenirs, and an authentic taste of everyday San José life.
Monumento Nacional / Parque Nacional
This bronze monument depicting Central America's fight against filibuster William Walker stands at the heart of a leafy downtown park popular with visitors.
Barrio Amón
This historic neighborhood of colorful Victorian and tropical mansions built by coffee elites is now a picturesque hub of boutique hotels and cafes.
Correos de Costa Rica (Central Post Office)
This grand early-20th-century building with its ornate clock tower remains one of downtown San José's most photographed architectural landmarks.
Museo Nacional de Costa Rica
Housed in a former fortress riddled with bullet holes from a 1948 battle, this museum traces Costa Rican history from pre-Columbian times to today.

train.note: Costa Rica has no international rail. INCOFER runs only commuter trains around Greater San José (to Heredia, Alajuela/Belén, Cartago and Pavas) on weekdays, not long-distance service.

intl.to: Managua (Nicaragua), Tegucigalpa & San Pedro Sula (Honduras), San Salvador, Guatemala City & Panama City

bus.note: International coaches leave from the operators' own terminals in San José, not a single bus station. Bring your passport; buses wait while everyone clears the Peñas Blancas (Nicaragua) or Paso Canoas (Panama) border.

ferry.note: No international ferries from Costa Rica. The main domestic passenger ferries run across the Gulf of Nicoya from Puntarenas (about 1.5h west of San José) to Paquera and Naranjo, operated by Naviera Tambor (https://navieratambor.com/).
